events.type: security incident at a customer (cyber claim naming Snowflake)
events.summary: At about 10:00 UK time (about 05:00 New York time) on Tuesday 6 October, hackers sent a push notification to users of the ASOS app (a large UK online fashion retailer that uses Snowflake): 'Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it', with a link to a Telegram channel of a previously unknown group calling itself 'Xuanye Group'. ASOS said: 'Basic personal information including name and contact details may have been accessed. We do not believe that payment-card information or account passwords, were impacted', and said it was investigating 'unauthorized activity involving third-party platforms' used for customer communications. Snowflake told Reuters and Bloomberg: 'At this time, we can report that we have found no compromise of the Snowflake platform', adding that the investigation is ongoing. ASOS has NOT confirmed that its Snowflake account was the source, has not named the third-party platform, and has not said how many customers are affected. The hackers gave no evidence; Bloomberg could not verify their claim. ASOS shares fell about 10% (Reuters); Snowflake fell about 2-3% before the open, then recovered (Bloomberg: 'little changed, after an earlier drop in premarket trading').
events.why_it_matters: Snowflake's business depends on companies trusting it with their most sensitive data. In 2024 a hacker used stolen customer passwords (not a flaw in Snowflake's own systems) to steal data from about 165 Snowflake customers, including Ticketmaster, AT&T and Santander; Snowflake then made multi-factor login mandatory (The Register). So any 'Snowflake breach' headline moves the stock even before facts are known. Today the evidence points away from Snowflake's platform: Snowflake found no compromise, and ASOS blamed third-party communication platforms. It would become a real problem only if an investigation showed a weakness in Snowflake itself.

why_chain.text: The pre-market drop lines up exactly with the ASOS push notification (about 10:00 UK = 05:00 New York) claiming hackers had 'fully compromised the Snowflake instance'. Reporters tied Snowflake's pre-market drop of about 2-3% to it.

The recovery before and at the open followed Snowflake's statement that it had 'found no compromise of the Snowflake platform'; Bloomberg described the stock as 'little changed, after an earlier drop in premarket trading'.

No published reason was found for the spike to $349 at the open or for the fade into the close: no Snowflake press release, no SEC filing, no analyst rating change in the window. Possible contributors: breach headlines kept coming all day (for example BleepingComputer at 12:33 New York: 'ASOS confirms data breach'), and software buyers were rotating into beaten-down names while SNOW is up about 125% in six months. These are guesses, not sourced causes.

Basic driver: investors are sensitive to any 'Snowflake breach' headline because of the 2024 campaign in which stolen customer logins were used to take data from about 165 Snowflake customers (Ticketmaster, AT&T, Santander). Snowflake's platform was not hacked then either, but the episode made trust a known risk for the stock.

Wednesday 2026-10-07 (close supplied by main session): $332.85, -0.92%. Market -0.24 points, software -1.32 points (IGV -1.19%), Snowflake's own part +0.64 (z 0.20). So Wednesday's fall was the whole software group falling, not Snowflake news; SNOW did slightly better than software. Why software fell on Wednesday was not researched (not available). Two days together: -1.81% from Monday's $338.99.

products.name: Snowflake AI Data Cloud account (a customer's 'instance')
products.what_it_is: Each customer gets its own private space on Snowflake (an 'instance' or account) where it stores its data (for a retailer: orders, customers, contact details) and runs analysis and AI on it.
products.analogy: Like a safe-deposit box in a bank vault: the bank (Snowflake) builds and guards the vault, but each customer holds its own keys. If a customer's key is stolen, its box can be opened without the vault itself being broken.
products.buyers: Large and mid-size companies; 829 of the Forbes Global 2000 and 828 customers each paying over $1 million a year (Q2 FY2027).
products.how_it_works: Customers load data into their account and pay for the computing they use to query it, like a taxi meter. Security is shared: Snowflake protects the platform; the customer controls who logs in. After the 2024 thefts (done with stolen customer passwords), Snowflake made multi-factor login mandatory.
products.price: Usage-based (pay for compute and storage used); list prices not researched today.
products.sales: Product revenue $1,491.9 million in Q2 FY2027 (quarter to 2026-07-31), +37% year over year; net revenue retention 126%; RPO $9.00 billion.
products.size_for_company: Essentially all of the company: product revenue was about 96% of total revenue ($1,491.9m of $1,546.8m) in Q2 FY2027 (calculation from the release).
products.competition: Databricks, and the cloud giants' own data warehouses (Amazon Redshift, Google BigQuery, Microsoft Fabric). Not researched further today.
products.why_investors_care: Trust is the product: customers put their most sensitive data in it. A proven weakness in Snowflake's own platform would hurt new sales and usage; a customer-side or third-party failure (what ASOS describes) mostly does not.
products.watch_next: Whether ASOS or investigators say the attackers got in through ASOS's Snowflake account, and if so how (stolen logins vs a Snowflake flaw); whether the Xuanye group leaks data or names other Snowflake customers; any Snowflake update.
